topic: Inflation: meaning (general price level, not one good), the rate formula with numbers, what 10% does over 20 years, types by rate band (creeping, walking, galloping, hyper), hyperinflation made concrete with bread and a 50 rupee note, and real cases (Zimbabwe 2008, Germany 1923, Venezuela 2019)

book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook defines inflation, explains how it is measured (index numbers), then lists the types by rate in rising order (creeping, walking, galloping, hyper), then causes and effects. Here the measure is one hand-sized example (5000 to 5500 = 10%), and an effect comes before any type: the same 10% is run for 20 years so the learner feels it (5000 to 33,638). The types are not given in rising order: creeping (good) and galloping (dangerous) are set up first as a contrast, and walking is filled in afterwards as the gap between them, which makes its meaning 'warning zone' obvious. Hyperinflation is then made concrete twice, first as a what-if with bread, then, after the learner's objection 'this is hypothetical' is voiced, with real cases. Causes are kept for the next video.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Cut the topic along one number, the inflation rate: first how the number is made and what one value of it does over time, then the number line split into bands, each band given a name, a verdict (good, alert, dangerous, extreme) and, for the extreme band, an everyday picture and real cases.

opening.what: No hook or agenda: straight into a plain-language definition (prices of goods and services rising year after year are called inflation), with goods and services icons and a rising price graph.

moves.concept: inflation = continuing rise in the general price level
moves.what: In everyday words: when prices of goods and services keep rising year after year, it is called inflation.

moves.concept: inflation = continuing rise in the general price level
moves.what: 'Inflation ka matlab': the general price level of goods and services in the economy keeps rising.

moves.concept: inflation = continuing rise in the general price level
moves.what: Stresses 'general price level' and corrects a likely wrong idea: if only one or two things get dearer, that is not inflation (egg panel struck on screen).
'Chaliye dekhte hain' how the rate of inflation is calculated.
'Maan lijiye' goods and services cost 5000 this year and 5500 next year.
Walks the formula in steps on the same numbers: subtract the earlier year's price level from the later one, divide by the earlier one, multiply by 100, giving 10%.

moves.concept: 10% a year compounds: 5000 to 33,638 in 20 years
moves.what: What does 10% mean? If 10% continues every year for 20 years, the same goods and services that cost 5000 in 2021 cost 33,638 in 2041.

moves.concept: 10% a year compounds: 5000 to 33,638 in 20 years
moves.what: So you can see how 10% inflation can make our goods and services expensive.
'But' inflation's effect is not always bad; in some cases it is good.
Inflation between 0 and 4% is called creeping inflation.
More precisely 2-4% is good: producers and traders earn reasonable profits, so investors want to invest, so economic growth is usually seen with it.
Between 10% and 50% it is called galloping inflation.
Honest note that books differ (some give 10-100%, some 10-200%), but in general 10-50% is used.
Recalls the 20-year graph from earlier in the same video: if 10% already raised prices that fast, 50% is very dangerous (part of this line falls in a transcript gap, 143.7-147.6 s).
Gives four other names in one breath: hopping, jumping, running and runaway inflation.
'Ab baat karte hain' the band between creeping and galloping, yaani 4 to 10%.
Inflation between 4 and 10% is called walking inflation.
Walking inflation works as an alert for the central bank and the government: if it is not controlled now it can turn into galloping, which is very dangerous.

moves.concept: rate bands as one scale: higher band, more danger
moves.what: So we see that as inflation rises it becomes more and more dangerous for the economy (bar turns green to red).

moves.concept: hyperinflation (>50%, prices rise daily, money loses value)
moves.what: 'Aisa nahin hai' that inflation stops at 50%; it can go higher.

moves.concept: hyperinflation (>50%, prices rise daily, money loses value)
moves.what: Above 50% it is called hyperinflation, the extreme form of inflation.

moves.concept: hyperinflation (>50%, prices rise daily, money loses value)
moves.what: Prices rise fast almost every day, inflation goes out of control, the yearly rate can reach millions, and the value of paper money keeps falling.

moves.concept: hyperinflation overnight: bread 50 to 1419, the 50 note buys one slice
moves.what: 'Sochke dekhiye': at 1,000,000% inflation, the bread packet that costs 50 rupees today would cost 1419 when you wake up tomorrow.

moves.concept: hyperinflation overnight: bread 50 to 1419, the 50 note buys one slice
moves.what: Same fact from the holder's side: today your 50 rupee note buys a whole packet, tomorrow the same note buys only a piece of bread.

moves.concept: hyperinflation overnight: bread 50 to 1419, the 50 note buys one slice
moves.what: This is what happens in hyperinflation: the value of your paper money and currency keeps falling.
Voices the learner's objection ('aap soch rahe honge'): this is a hypothetical case, where would 1 million % ever happen? Answer: it does.
Zimbabwe 2008: yearly inflation given as 90 billion million percent, and a bread packet cost 3.5 crore Zimbabwe dollars (figures to check).
'Sochke dekhiye': if bread needs 3.5 crore, other things must have needed thousands of crores.
So the government printed notes up to 100 million dollars, yet they had no value; a news magazine called the currency worthless.
Not only Zimbabwe: Germany in 1923 after the First World War and Venezuela recently in 2019.
One line: today we understood what inflation is.
Next video: cost-push and demand-pull inflation, to see why inflation happens at all.

examples.what: Eggs on screen: one or two goods getting dearer, tagged 'not inflation'.
examples.carries: inflation means the general price level, not one price

examples.what: Goods and services 5000 rupees in 2021, 5500 in 2022; the formula gives 10%.
10% every year for 20 years: 5000 rupees in 2021 becomes 33,638 in 2041.
examples.carries: what a yearly rate does over time; later reused to argue that 50% is dangerous

examples.what: At 1,000,000% a 50 rupee bread packet costs 1419 rupees next morning (arithmetic doubtful, see checks).
examples.carries: hyperinflation as prices that change overnight

examples.what: The same 50 rupee note buys a whole packet today and one slice tomorrow.
Zimbabwe 2008: huge yearly rate, bread at 3.5 crore Zimbabwe dollars, 100 million dollar notes, currency called worthless.
Germany 1923 after the First World War; Venezuela 2019.
examples.carries: hyperinflation has happened in several countries

closing.what: A one-line recap ('today we understood what inflation is') and then a teaser for the next video on cost-push and demand-pull inflation; no recap of the bands on screen.

narration.density: About 9 core terms (inflation, general price level, rate of inflation, creeping, galloping, walking, hyperinflation, extreme form, value of paper money) plus 4 aliases for galloping and 2 next-video terms, in about 370 s of teaching: about 1.5 core terms per minute (2.2 with aliases). Comfortable for class 9 to UPSC basics; the only burst is the four aliases in one breath at 167 s.

talmel_summary: Numbers and years land together with their spoken words (5000, 5500, 4%, 90, 1923, 2019), and the best moments are pictures that carry the meaning: the bar repainting green to red as danger rises, and the same 50 rupee note buying a packet today and a slice tomorrow. When the picture leads it is mostly by 1-2.5 s, but the coloured explanation notes pop in whole and are read out over the next 6-16 s, and the Zimbabwe map appears about 4 s before the objection it answers is finished. Walking inflation's alert role, the formula's steps and the reasons why a band is good or dangerous are carried only by speech or by text.

voice.notes: About 176 words per minute, brisk and even, with almost no pauses (one 4 s gap at 143.7 s and one stretched pause near 318-331 s). Explanatory tone using 'maan lijiye', 'yaani', 'sochke dekhiye', 'aap soch rahe honge', 'aisa nahin hai'. Stress falls on 'general price level', 'dangerous', 'extreme form' and on the big numbers. Numbers are read in full (5000, 5500, 33,638, 1419); large values switch between the Indian and the international system (crore for Zimbabwe dollars, million and billion for rates), which may confuse a learner without a note.

game_ideas.player_does: Sets the yearly inflation rate with a slider on the 'INFLATION %' bar and presses 'next year' to run a 20-year town economy holding a 5000 rupee basket.
game_ideas.process_happens: The basket's price tag ticks up every year on a timeline; the bar zone lights (creeping green, walking amber with an alarm at the central bank, galloping brown, hyper red); producers' profit and investor icons rise or leave depending on the zone.
game_ideas.win: Keep the rate in the 2-4% zone for 20 years: profits and investment grow and the basket price rises gently.
game_ideas.lose: Above 10% the basket races past 33,638 rupees by year 20 and investors leave; above 50% a saved 50 rupee note buys only a slice of bread the next day.
game_ideas.concept: rate bands as one scale: higher band, more danger

game_ideas.player_does: Fills the inflation formula from a shop bill (last year's and this year's price) by dragging numbers into the slots, then checks a classmate's worked answer for the mistake.
game_ideas.process_happens: The marker on the inflation scale moves to the computed rate and the zone name lights up.
game_ideas.win: Correct slots: (new - old) / old x 100, and the marker lands in the right band.
game_ideas.lose: Dividing by the new price gives 9.09% instead of 10%, and the marker lands short, showing why the base must be the old price.

game_ideas.player_does: Sorts market scenes into 'inflation' and 'not inflation': only onions dearer; almost every price up 6% a year; one phone cheaper while everything else rises; prices doubling every week.
game_ideas.process_happens: A general price level meter rises only for scenes where most prices rise; the band name appears for real inflation cases.
game_ideas.win: All scenes sorted, with the right band named for the inflation scenes.
game_ideas.lose: Calling 'only onions dearer' inflation leaves the general price level meter flat, showing that one price is not the price level.
game_ideas.concept: inflation = continuing rise in the general price level

game_ideas.player_does: Holds a 50 rupee note in a market during hyperinflation and decides each hour whether to buy bread now or wait.
game_ideas.process_happens: Price tags on the stall change every hour; the bread the note can buy shrinks from a packet to a slice.
game_ideas.win: Buy early and see why people rush to spend money in hyperinflation.
game_ideas.lose: Waiting leaves the same note buying a slice: the note did not change, its value did.
game_ideas.concept: hyperinflation overnight: bread 50 to 1419, the 50 note buys one slice

checks_learned: A price derived from a yearly rate over a shorter period (next morning, next month) must be recomputed by code with compounding; flag a value that matches simple division of the yearly rise (50 + 50 x 10,000/365 = 1419 here, while compounding gives about 51).
A threshold in a definition must carry its period on screen (hyperinflation: 50% per month in the usual definition, not per year).
Record-event figures (peak inflation rate, largest note printed) must be checked against a dated facts table before use; flag figures with mixed units such as 'billion million'.
Every band on a classification scale needs a label plus one picture of its effect; a band with only a label (walking here) leaves its spoken meaning unshown.
A formula shown with numbers should light each operation on its spoken word (subtract, divide, multiply), not fade in whole.
When the narration voices a learner's objection, the answer picture must not appear before the objection is finished (the map here leads by about 4 s).
Explanation text boxes should not pop in whole and then be read for 6-16 s; reveal them line by line with the speech or replace them with a picture of the effect.
When books give different ranges, the chosen range and a 'books differ' tag should be on screen, not only in speech.
Do not mix crore and million or billion in one example without a conversion note for Hindi-medium learners.

teaching_best.why: the misconception 'one or two goods dearer = inflation' is named and corrected right after the definition, with a non-example on screen
the computed 10% is run for 20 years (5000 to 33,638), turning a percent into a felt price; the same chart is recalled at 150 s to argue why 50% is dangerous
walking inflation is taught last, as the gap between good and dangerous, so 'alert zone' needs no extra explanation
the hyperinflation example is reframed from price to money: the same 50 rupee note buys a packet today and one slice tomorrow
the learner's objection 'this is only hypothetical' is voiced and answered with real cases
says openly that books give different ranges and which one is used

teaching_weak.why: why 2-4% is good is a stated chain (profit, investment, growth) with no example or numbers
walking inflation's 'alert' role is told without who does what when the alarm rings
1419 rupees next morning is doubtful arithmetic (simple daily division of the yearly rise)
the Zimbabwe figures ('90 billion million %', notes 'up to 100 million') are doubtful or incomplete and are given without a source
four alias names are given in one breath with no reason for any of them
the recap is one spoken line; the four bands are not recapped as a whole
